Information since May points to solid employment and moderate growth, but soft business investment and inflation below 2 percent. Holding the federal funds rate at 2.25–2.50 percent while signaling readiness to act is consistent with risk-management under heightened uncertainty and a flatter Phillips curve with anchored expectations; the decline in market-based inflation compensation aligns with lower term premia.

FSR context tempers the outlook. The FSR links economic fundamentals to market liquidity and valuations, noting that falling 10-year Treasury yields support elevated asset valuations and lower capitalization rates, while investor appetite appears stronger for Treasuries than for corporate credit at times, indicating a cautious risk tone. Corporate-sector vulnerabilities matter: leveraged loans are sensitive to credit standards, and high business leverage can amplify a capex slowdown. On the household side, balances held by near-prime and subprime borrowers highlight pockets of cyclical risk. These stability considerations reinforce a dovish bias despite still-firm activity.

Operationally, use of interest on reserves and the ON RRP to maintain the target range is consistent with the floor-system framework, and ongoing supervisory rigor (including stress testing) supports resilience even as market liquidity and valuations remain sensitive to fundamentals.

Net tone: growth and labor are steady, inflation is soft, and the FSR adds caution via valuation and credit vulnerabilities. Dovish on risks, modestly positive on activity.
